=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer-Side Review of Seller's SPA Positions and Disclosure Letter

## Preliminary point: the "FINAL / agreed at principal level" framing

The covering note says these positions were "settled at principal level by both deal teams," are "marked FINAL" and are "not intended to be re-opened." It also says the caps, baskets and knowledge qualifiers are "standard and widely accepted market terms."

**Treat all of this as Seller advocacy, not fact.** We have nothing showing that Wattlebridge's principals agreed to these terms. Several positions, such as title under the general cap and limitations applying to fraud, are not market for a buyer in any event. Please confirm with your principals what, if anything, was agreed commercially. Unless they confirm otherwise, every point below remains open for mark-up.

The Seller's own Disclosure Letter also contradicts parts of its SPA cover note:
- Bluefen consent is said to be "addressed," but no consent has been obtained.
- Ironquay is said to be "adequate," but there is no payment evidence and no assignment.
- DD-006 is said to be "not expected to be material," but the investigation is preliminary and its scope is unknown.

That gap is itself a negotiating point.

---

## Part A: Liability regime

### 1. General cap, cl 12.1 (20% / AUD 4.8m)
- **Issue:** 20% is within a range some buyers accept for general warranties. However, the Seller wants this cap to cover *everything*, including title, tax and specific indemnities (see items 4–6). The known exposures alone are material relative to AUD 4.8m: Riverlark AUD 3.2m, bonuses AUD 420k plus on-costs, Ironquay IP, the privacy incident, and Bluefen at ~30% of revenue.
- **Push back:**
  - Accept a general-warranty cap only if fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities, leakage/price adjustment, covenants and fraud sit outside it.
  - Fundamental warranties and tax should be capped at 100% of price.
  - Consider seeking 25–30% for general warranties as an opening position, or pairing a lower cap with W&I insurance (see item 20).

### 2. Thresholds, cl 12.2 (de minimis AUD 25k; basket AUD 250k as a deductible)
- **Issue:** The basket is ~1.04% of price and operates as a **deductible** ("only the excess… is recoverable"). The Seller would therefore never bear the first AUD 250k of valid claims.
- **Push back:**
  - Make it a **tipping basket**, so that once the threshold is exceeded the claim is recoverable from dollar one.
  - Reduce it to ~0.5% (AUD 120k).
  - Reduce the de minimis to ~AUD 10–15k, and aggregate related or same-cause claims when testing it.
  - Thresholds should not apply to tax, fundamental warranties, specific indemnities, leakage or fraud.

### 3. Time limits, cl 12.3/13 (18 months; "applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise")
- **Issue:** 18 months for general warranties is arguable, but the catch-all wording quietly applies 18 months to title, tax and indemnities.
- **Push back:**
  - **General warranties:** 24 months, so that two full audit cycles post-Completion are covered.
  - **Tax:** at least the ATO amendment period plus a buffer. Typically 5–7 years, with no limit for fraud or evasion.
  - **Title/capacity:** 7 years, or the statutory limitation period. If the SPA is executed as a deed, the NSW period is 12 years.
  - **Specific indemnities:** tailored periods, for example running until the relevant claim or regulatory window closes.
  - Reverse the default: limitations apply **only where expressly stated**.

### 4. Fundamental / title warranties under the same cap and time limits
- **Issue:** This is not market. If title or capacity fails, the Buyer has not received what it paid for, so loss can equal the whole price.
- **Push back:** Reject this. Cap at 100% of price, apply a long time limit, and remove the basket and de minimis. Title must not be qualified by disclosure.

### 5. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature," cl 9.3/12.8/20.5
- **Issue:** As drafted, this would purport to limit liability for **fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment**. That is unacceptable and is generally unenforceable as to fraud in any case. It would also restrict claims for misleading or deceptive conduct (ACL s 18) and for breach of covenants such as pre-Completion conduct and restraints.
- **Push back:** Carve out of all limitations and of the exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions:
  - fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment by the Seller, the Company or their agents;
  - fundamental warranties;
  - tax;
  - specific indemnities;
  - leakage and price adjustment;
  - covenant breaches;
  - equitable remedies such as specific performance and injunction.

  Non-reliance should be limited to statements outside the SPA, the Disclosure Letter and written replies to DD requests.

### 6. Tax / IP "settled under the general regime"
- **Issue:** Folding tax into general warranties means tax claims would be subject to the basket, the 4.8m cap and an 18-month limit. That is far shorter than the ATO's ability to amend assessments.
- **Push back:**
  - A standalone **tax indemnity** for pre-Completion tax: dollar-one recovery, capped at price, with tax-specific time limits and conduct-of-claims provisions.
  - IP is core value for a SaaS target, so IP warranties should have an elevated cap and a longer period, or be treated as quasi-fundamental.

---

## Part B: Disclosure and knowledge

### 7. General disclosure of the data room and public registers (Schedule 7; DL 1.1–1.2)
- **Issue:** This would qualify every warranty against everything in the data room and in public records, whether or not the Buyer could identify the relevant issue. It reverses the purpose of warranties. The data room snapshot is also dated **22 September 2026**, which is already ~6 weeks old, and anything added later is unclear.
- **Push back:**
  - Accept **specific disclosures only**, made against particular warranties, with a **fair disclosure** standard: sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature *and scope* of the matter.
  - Reject the general data room and public-records disclosure. At most, accept a narrowly defined set of specified searches, such as ASIC, PPSR and court searches on a stated date.
  - Disclosure must not qualify fundamental warranties, tax, or any specific indemnity.
  - The Seller must not be able to disclose new matters against the Completion repetition of warranties without triggering Buyer rights, such as termination or an indemnity.

### 8. Buyer knowledge, cl 8.3
- **Issue:** This is extremely broad. It extends to the knowledge of **advisers** and to anything **"discoverable"** (constructive knowledge). Combined with item 7, it would effectively wipe out warranty protection for anything in the data room.
- **Push back:** Reject the clause. The preferred position is that the Buyer's rights are not affected by any knowledge, actual, constructive or imputed, other than matters fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter. A fallback is actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals (not advisers) that the specific matter amounted to a warranty breach.

### 9. Disclosure Letter non-admission, DL 1.4, and reservation, DL 11
- **Issue:** Non-admission language is common. However, DL 11 ("Buyer must evaluate…") reinforces the constructive-knowledge approach.
- **Push back:** Accept non-admission only if it is clear that the disclosures do not limit the specific indemnities or any Seller obligation. Delete DL 11, or limit it to a statement that the DL is not a warranty in itself.

---

## Part C: Deal-specific issues

### 10. Bluefen consent, cl 3/6.3 (~AUD 3.6m, ~30% of FY26 revenue)
- **Issue:** DL 2 confirms that no consent has been obtained and there is no evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied. The Seller offers only "reasonable endeavours" and would treat the condition as satisfied on *any* written consent, even one that is conditional or imposes new terms.
- **Push back:**
  - Make Bluefen consent a **condition precedent for the Buyer's benefit**, waivable only by the Buyer. It should be satisfied only by an unconditional written consent, or one on terms acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably, with evidence that all cl 11.3 conditions are met.
  - The Seller should give a "best endeavours" or "all reasonable endeavours" obligation, with the Buyer having review and input on approaches to Bluefen.
  - The Buyer should have a walk right if the consent is not obtained by the sunset date.
  - Consider a fallback: a price adjustment, earn-out or escrow if Bluefen terminates or renegotiates within 12 months of Completion.

### 11. Riverlark facility, cl 2/7 (~AUD 3.2m; release "following Completion")
- **Issue:** The deal is debt-free/cash-free, yet the Seller proposes a post-Completion release. DL 3 confirms the debt is unpaid and there is no discharge. The change-control clause (8.1) may trigger default or acceleration on Completion, and the Company's assets would remain encumbered.
- **Push back:**
  - The Seller must deliver at Completion a **payout letter** and a **deed of release**, with PPSR financing-change statements and any registered security discharges to be lodged immediately.
  - The facility should be repaid from the purchase price through the funds flow as Indebtedness.
  - This should be a Completion deliverable and a CP, backed by an uncapped specific indemnity for any facility liability.

### 12. Completion bonuses, DD-005 (AUD 420k, omitted from the funds flow)
- **Issue:** The Seller says these are "a matter for the Seller," but the **Company is the employer** and the legal obligor. Leaving them out of the funds flow means the Buyer would effectively fund them after Completion. On-costs are also not addressed (DL 5) and may include:
  - PAYG withholding;
  - superannuation guarantee (12% since 1 July 2025), to the extent the bonuses are ordinary time earnings;
  - NSW payroll tax, if the Company is above the threshold;
  - workers' compensation premiums.
- **Push back:**
  - Treat the bonuses plus all on-costs as **Indebtedness or Transaction Costs** and deduct them from the price.
  - Pay them through Company payroll at or immediately after Completion, funded from the Seller's proceeds.
  - Back this with a specific indemnity outside the cap and thresholds.
  - Obtain the bonus letters to confirm the amounts and conditions.

### 13. Ironquay IP, cl 11.1 (SOW3; AUD 180k open)
- **Issue:** The real risk is **ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials**, not the AUD 180k fee. Under DD-004 cl 7.3, title does not pass until every SOW3 fee is paid in cleared funds. DL 4 confirms there is no payment receipt and no confirmatory assignment. If the materials are in the product, the Company may not own its own code, and infringement claims are possible. Limiting the indemnity to "the specific SOW3 payment" is inadequate.
- **Push back:**
  - Add a CP or Completion deliverable: evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees plus a **confirmatory IP assignment deed** from Ironquay. Alternatively, the Seller procures payment from its own funds before Completion.
  - Broaden the indemnity to cover all loss from any failure of the Company to own the SOW3 Project Materials, or any Ironquay claim (fees, infringement, injunction, re-engineering costs). It should sit outside the cap, basket and general time limit.
  - The IP warranties must not be qualified by the Ironquay disclosure.

### 14. Export / privacy incident, cl 4.6/Schedule 6, DD-006 (~1,240 records)
- **Issue:** The Seller calls this a "preliminary operational matter… not expected to be material." Its own DL 6 says the following are all unknown: whether there was access, the scope, and whether notification is required. Names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps are likely personal information under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth).
  - If the incident is an eligible data breach, the NDB scheme requires an assessment within 30 days of awareness (s 26WH) and notification of the OAIC and affected individuals.
  - The incident pre-dates 22 September, so that window may already have closed.
  - Penalties for serious interferences with privacy are now very significant.
  - There is also potential exposure to customer contract claims, particularly if records belong to customers' users, and to reputational harm.
- **Push back:**
  - Require the full incident file now: timeline, logs, link access records, forensic findings, the assessment under s 26WH, and any notifications or customer communications.
  - Add a pre-Completion covenant to complete the investigation and make any required notifications, with Buyer consultation.
  - Add a **specific indemnity** for all losses from the incident, including regulatory penalties to the extent lawfully indemnifiable, investigation and remediation costs, customer claims and notification costs. It should sit outside the cap and thresholds and run for at least 3–4 years.
  - Consider a **retention or escrow** pending resolution.
  - The privacy and data-security warranties must not be qualified by DD-006.

### 15. Sandbar supplier renewals, DD-008/DD-011 (3 × AUD 110k = AUD 330k)
- **Issue:** These are three "related" renewals that the Seller wants read together but describes as ordinary course. Several questions are unanswered:
  - Were they split to stay under a materiality, approval or conduct-of-business threshold?
  - Is Sandbar a related party of the Seller? If so, payments could be **leakage**.
  - Are the renewals terminable, and have the costs been accrued?
- **Push back:**
  - Request the contracts, approval history and any relationship between Sandbar and the Seller.
  - If any renewal was entered into after the accounts date or locked-box date, or without board approval, treat it as requiring Buyer consent under the interim covenants.
  - Any amount that is a related-party payment should be leakage, recoverable dollar for dollar.
  - Unaccrued committed amounts should be treated as a debt-like item.
  - Add a warranty that no material contract was split or structured to avoid thresholds.

### 16. Title, DD-012 (share register only)
- **Issue:** A Company-maintained register is not sufficient comfort on its own. DL 10 expressly notes that the Buyer has not verified it.
- **Push back:**
  - **Verify independently:** ASIC company extract and historical share issues, share certificates, issuance resolutions, PPSR searches against the Seller over the shares, and confirmation that there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs, ESOP awards or other rights to shares.
  - Add warranties of full legal and beneficial title, free of encumbrances.
  - Completion deliverables should include signed share transfers, original certificates (or a lost-certificate indemnity), any required releases from the Seller's own financiers, and waivers of pre-emptive rights.

### 17. Office lease, DD-007, and Mossvale, DD-009
- **Issue:** The Seller characterises both as not requiring consent to a share sale. That is the Seller's reading.
- **Push back:**
  - Review both documents ourselves. Check whether the "assignment" definitions deem a change of control to be an assignment.
  - The lease notification obligation must be complied with as a Completion deliverable or covenant.
  - Seek a warranty that no consent is required under any material contract other than those listed, with an indemnity if that proves wrong.

---

## Part D: Credit and recovery protection

### 18. Seller covenant strength
Harbourglass Ventures appears to be a venture vehicle and may distribute sale proceeds to its investors soon after Completion. In that case, warranty and indemnity rights may be worth little.
- **Push back:** Seek an **escrow or retention**, for example 10–15% of price for 18–24 months, with specific holdbacks for the privacy incident and Ironquay. Alternatively, seek a parent or fund guarantee, or W&I insurance (item 20).

### 19. Signing to Completion
- **Push back:**
  - Warranties should be repeated at Completion.
  - Add customary interim conduct covenants with Buyer consent rights, including over new supplier commitments (relevant to Sandbar), employee bonuses and data incidents.
  - Add an obligation to notify the Buyer of breaches, with a Buyer termination right for material breach or material adverse change.
  - Obtain an updated data room index and DL dated at signing, not 22 September.

### 20. W&I insurance (option)
- **Consideration:** If the Seller insists on a low cap, a buy-side W&I policy can bridge the gap. However, known matters such as Bluefen, Riverlark, the bonuses, Ironquay and DD-006 will be **excluded** from cover. They must therefore be dealt with through CPs, price mechanics, specific indemnities and escrow regardless.

---

## Summary of recommendations

| # | Item | Seller position | Buyer recommendation | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| — | "FINAL" framing | Not to be re-opened | Disregard unless our principals confirm; all points open | High |
| 1 | General cap | 20% for all claims | 20–30% for general warranties only; carve-outs uncapped or at 100% | High |
| 2 | Basket / de minimis | AUD 250k deductible; AUD 25k | Tipping basket ~AUD 120k; de minimis AUD 10–15k with aggregation | Medium |
| 3 | Time limits | 18 months for everything | 24 months general; tax 5–7 years; title 7+ years; indemnities tailored | High |
| 4 | Fundamental / title | Same cap and time | 100% of price, long period, not disclosable | High |
| 5 | Limitations / non-reliance | All claims incl. fraud | Carve out fraud, fundamental, tax, indemnities, leakage, covenants | High |
| 6 | Tax / IP | General regime | Standalone tax indemnity; enhanced IP protection | High |
| 7 | General disclosure | Data room plus public records | Specific, fair disclosure only; no qualification of fundamental, tax or indemnities | High |
| 8 | Buyer knowledge | Advisers plus "discoverable" | Delete, or actual knowledge of named individuals only | High |
| 10 | Bluefen | Reasonable endeavours; any consent | Buyer CP; unconditional or acceptable consent plus cl 11.3 evidence; walk right | High |
| 11 | Riverlark | Release post-Completion | Payout plus release plus PPSR discharge at Completion, paid via funds flow | High |
| 12 | Bonuses | Off funds flow | Debt-like deduction incl. super, payroll tax, PAYG; indemnity | High |
| 13 | Ironquay | Fee-only indemnity | Payment evidence plus confirmatory assignment as CP; broad uncapped IP indemnity | High |
| 14 | DD-006 privacy | "Not material" | Full file; NDB assessment; specific indemnity; escrow | High |
| 15 | Sandbar | Ordinary course | Diligence; leakage or debt-like treatment if applicable; anti-splitting warranty | Medium |
| 16 | Title | Register only | Independent verification plus full title warranties and deliverables | High |
| 17 | Lease / Mossvale | No consent needed | Verify ourselves; consents warranty plus indemnity | Medium |
| 18 | Recovery | None offered | Escrow 10–15% and/or guarantee; consider W&I | High |
| 19 | Interim period | Silent | Repetition, interim covenants, updated DL at signing | Medium |

**Immediate next steps:**
1. Confirm with Wattlebridge principals what, if anything, was actually agreed commercially.
2. Issue supplementary DD requests covering: the DD-006 incident file, Ironquay payment records, the Bluefen correspondence, the Riverlark payout figure and security list, the bonus letters, the Sandbar contracts and relationship, and the cap table and ASIC records.
3. Prepare the SPA mark-up on the positions above, with specific indemnities and escrow as the structural backstop for the known issues.

*This analysis is based solely on the Seller's summary documents. The underlying SPA text and DD documents should be reviewed before the mark-up is finalised.*

  - IP is core value for a SaaS target, so IP warranties should have an elevated cap and a longer period, or be treated as quasi-fundamental.

## Part B: Disclosure and knowledge

### 7. General disclosure of the data room and public registers (Schedule 7; DL 1.1–1.2)
- **Issue:** This would qualify every warranty against everything in the data room and in public records, whether or not the Buyer could identify the relevant issue. It reverses the purpose of warranties. The data room snapshot is also dated **22 September 2026**, which is already ~6 weeks old, and anything added later is unclear.
- **Push back:**
  - Accept **specific disclosures only**, made against particular warranties, with a **fair disclosure** standard: sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature *and scope* of the matter.
  - Reject the general data room and public-records disclosure. At most, accept a narrowly defined set of specified searches, such as ASIC, PPSR and court searches on a stated date.
  - Disclosure must not qualify fundamental warranties, tax, or any specific indemnity.
  - The Seller must not be able to disclose new matters against the Completion repetition of warranties without triggering Buyer rights, such as termination or an indemnity.

### 8. Buyer knowledge, cl 8.3
- **Issue:** This is extremely broad. It extends to the knowledge of **advisers** and to anything **"discoverable"** (constructive knowledge). Combined with item 7, it would effectively wipe out warranty protection for anything in the data room.
- **Push back:** Reject the clause. The preferred position is that the Buyer's rights are not affected by any knowledge, actual, constructive or imputed, other than matters fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter. A fallback is actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals (not advisers) that the specific matter amounted to a warranty breach.

### 9. Disclosure Letter non-admission, DL 1.4, and reservation, DL 11
- **Issue:** Non-admission language is common. However, DL 11 ("Buyer must evaluate…") reinforces the constructive-knowledge approach.
- **Push back:** Accept non-admission only if it is clear that the disclosures do not limit the specific indemnities or any Seller obligation. Delete DL 11, or limit it to a statement that the DL is not a warranty in itself.

## Part C: Deal-specific issues

### 10. Bluefen consent, cl 3/6.3 (~AUD 3.6m, ~30% of FY26 revenue)
- **Issue:** DL 2 confirms that no consent has been obtained and there is no evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied. The Seller offers only "reasonable endeavours" and would treat the condition as satisfied on *any* written consent, even one that is conditional or imposes new terms.
- **Push back:**
  - Make Bluefen consent a **condition precedent for the Buyer's benefit**, waivable only by the Buyer. It should be satisfied only by an unconditional written consent, or one on terms acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably, with evidence that all cl 11.3 conditions are met.
  - The Seller should give a "best endeavours" or "all reasonable endeavours" obligation, with the Buyer having review and input on approaches to Bluefen.
  - The Buyer should have a walk right if the consent is not obtained by the sunset date.
  - Consider a fallback: a price adjustment, earn-out or escrow if Bluefen terminates or renegotiates within 12 months of Completion.

### 11. Riverlark facility, cl 2/7 (~AUD 3.2m; release "following Completion")
- **Issue:** The deal is debt-free/cash-free, yet the Seller proposes a post-Completion release. DL 3 confirms the debt is unpaid and there is no discharge. The change-control clause (8.1) may trigger default or acceleration on Completion, and the Company's assets would remain encumbered.
- **Push back:**
  - The Seller must deliver at Completion a **payout letter** and a **deed of release**, with PPSR financing-change statements and any registered security discharges to be lodged immediately.
  - The facility should be repaid from the purchase price through the funds flow as Indebtedness.
  - This should be a Completion deliverable and a CP, backed by an uncapped specific indemnity for any facility liability.

### 12. Completion bonuses, DD-005 (AUD 420k, omitted from the funds flow)
- **Issue:** The Seller says these are "a matter for the Seller," but the **Company is the employer** and the legal obligor. Leaving them out of the funds flow means the Buyer would effectively fund them after Completion. On-costs are also not addressed (DL 5) and may include:
  - PAYG withholding;
  - superannuation guarantee (12% since 1 July 2025), to the extent the bonuses are ordinary time earnings;
  - NSW payroll tax, if the Company is above the threshold;
  - workers' compensation premiums.
- **Push back:**
  - Treat the bonuses plus all on-costs as **Indebtedness or Transaction Costs** and deduct them from the price.
  - Pay them through Company payroll at or immediately after Completion, funded from the Seller's proceeds.
  - Back this with a specific indemnity outside the cap and thresholds.
  - Obtain the bonus letters to confirm the amounts and conditions.

### 13. Ironquay IP, cl 11.1 (SOW3; AUD 180k open)
- **Issue:** The real risk is **ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials**, not the AUD 180k fee. Under DD-004 cl 7.3, title does not pass until every SOW3 fee is paid in cleared funds. DL 4 confirms there is no payment receipt and no confirmatory assignment. If the materials are in the product, the Company may not own its own code, and infringement claims are possible. Limiting the indemnity to "the specific SOW3 payment" is inadequate.
- **Push back:**
  - Add a CP or Completion deliverable: evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees plus a **confirmatory IP assignment deed** from Ironquay. Alternatively, the Seller procures payment from its own funds before Completion.
  - Broaden the indemnity to cover all loss from any failure of the Company to own the SOW3 Project Materials, or any Ironquay claim (fees, infringement, injunction, re-engineering costs). It should sit outside the cap, basket and general time limit.
  - The IP warranties must not be qualified by the Ironquay disclosure.

### 14. Export / privacy incident, cl 4.6/Schedule 6, DD-006 (~1,240 records)
- **Issue:** The Seller calls this a "preliminary operational matter… not expected to be material." Its own DL 6 says the following are all unknown: whether there was access, the scope, and whether notification is required. Names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps are likely personal information under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth).
  - If the incident is an eligible data breach, the NDB scheme requires an assessment within 30 days of awareness (s 26WH) and notification of the OAIC and affected individuals.
  - The incident pre-dates 22 September, so that window may already have closed.
  - Penalties for serious interferences with privacy are now very significant.
  - There is also potential exposure to customer contract claims, particularly if records belong to customers' users, and to reputational harm.
- **Push back:**
  - Require the full incident file now: timeline, logs, link access records, forensic findings, the assessment under s 26WH, and any notifications or customer communications.
  - Add a pre-Completion covenant to complete the investigation and make any required notifications, with Buyer consultation.
  - Add a **specific indemnity** for all losses from the incident, including regulatory penalties to the extent lawfully indemnifiable, investigation and remediation costs, customer claims and notification costs. It should sit outside the cap and thresholds and run for at least 3–4 years.
  - Consider a **retention or escrow** pending resolution.
  - The privacy and data-security warranties must not be qualified by DD-006.

### 15. Sandbar supplier renewals, DD-008/DD-011 (3 × AUD 110k = AUD 330k)
- **Issue:** These are three "related" renewals that the Seller wants read together but describes as ordinary course. Several questions are unanswered:
  - Were they split to stay under a materiality, approval or conduct-of-business threshold?
  - Is Sandbar a related party of the Seller? If so, payments could be **leakage**.
  - Are the renewals terminable, and have the costs been accrued?
- **Push back:**
  - Request the contracts, approval history and any relationship between Sandbar and the Seller.
  - If any renewal was entered into after the accounts date or locked-box date, or without board approval, treat it as requiring Buyer consent under the interim covenants.
  - Any amount that is a related-party payment should be leakage, recoverable dollar for dollar.
  - Unaccrued committed amounts should be treated as a debt-like item.
  - Add a warranty that no material contract was split or structured to avoid thresholds.

### 16. Title, DD-012 (share register only)
- **Issue:** A Company-maintained register is not sufficient comfort on its own. DL 10 expressly notes that the Buyer has not verified it.
- **Push back:**
  - **Verify independently:** ASIC company extract and historical share issues, share certificates, issuance resolutions, PPSR searches against the Seller over the shares, and confirmation that there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs, ESOP awards or other rights to shares.
  - Add warranties of full legal and beneficial title, free of encumbrances.
  - Completion deliverables should include signed share transfers, original certificates (or a lost-certificate indemnity), any required releases from the Seller's own financiers, and waivers of pre-emptive rights.

### 17. Office lease, DD-007, and Mossvale, DD-009
- **Issue:** The Seller characterises both as not requiring consent to a share sale. That is the Seller's reading.
- **Push back:**
  - Review both documents ourselves. Check whether the "assignment" definitions deem a change of control to be an assignment.
  - The lease notification obligation must be complied with as a Completion deliverable or covenant.
  - Seek a warranty that no consent is required under any material contract other than those listed, with an indemnity if that proves wrong.

## Part D: Credit and recovery protection

### 18. Seller covenant strength
Harbourglass Ventures appears to be a venture vehicle and may distribute sale proceeds to its investors soon after Completion. In that case, warranty and indemnity rights may be worth little.
- **Push back:** Seek an **escrow or retention**, for example 10–15% of price for 18–24 months, with specific holdbacks for the privacy incident and Ironquay. Alternatively, seek a parent or fund guarantee, or W&I insurance (item 20).

### 19. Signing to Completion
- **Push back:**
  - Warranties should be repeated at Completion.
  - Add customary interim conduct covenants with Buyer consent rights, including over new supplier commitments (relevant to Sandbar), employee bonuses and data incidents.
  - Add an obligation to notify the Buyer of breaches, with a Buyer termination right for material breach or material adverse change.
  - Obtain an updated data room index and DL dated at signing, not 22 September.

### 20. W&I insurance (option)
- **Consideration:** If the Seller insists on a low cap, a buy-side W&I policy can bridge the gap. However, known matters such as Bluefen, Riverlark, the bonuses, Ironquay and DD-006 will be **excluded** from cover. They must therefore be dealt with through CPs, price mechanics, specific indemnities and escrow regardless.
